{#hfwt} # 1. Introduction

{#hfqz} Proximal femoral fractures (PFFs) occur around the hip joint in the upper femur bone. The femoral head, neck, and intertrochanteric/subtrochanteric fractures are the main subcategories based on their location . PFFs, one of the most common presentations to emergency departments (ED), usually occur because of falls and are more likely to be seen in the elderly, especially in patients with osteoporosis [1]. Mortality and morbidity prediction is a difficult issue for physicians, and various scoring systems have been developed. One of these scoring systems is the hemoglobin, albumin, lymphocyte and, platelet (HALP) score, which is a composite score used to assess the nutritional and immune status of a patient. It is considered a prognostic indicator and has been used to predict overall survival and other outcomes in various cancers and non-cancer diseases [2–6]. The HALP score, which is expressed as hemoglobin (g/L) × albumin (g/L) × lymphocyte (/L) / platelet (/L), was first used to predict the prognosis of gastric carcinoma by Chen et al. in 2015. In this study, low HALP score was reported as an indicator of poor prognosis [6]. In this respect, HALP scoring as a composite immunonutritional biomarker shows promise in assessing a patient’s overall health status by integrating several routinely collected laboratory indicators.

ops.markdown: This study has several important limitations. First, its retrospective observational design means that a direct causal relationship between HALP scores and mortality could not be established. Second, potential confounding variables that may affect mortality outcomes in specific subgroups were not addressed: differences in demographics (such as age, sex, and ethnicity) and surgical techniques might have significantly influenced the observed outcomes, and factors related to rehabilitation, medication use, nutritional status, and psychosocial aspects were not analyzed in detail. These unaccounted variables may limit the generalizability of our findings, suggesting that the observed associations should be interpreted with caution. Future studies should incorporate these factors to enhance our understanding of the relationship between HALP score and mortality risk in elderly patients with hip fractures. Moreover, more comprehensive and longer-term prospective cohort studies are required to confirm the causal relationship between HALP levels and long-term mortality. Third, the fact that this study was conducted at a single center may also restrict the generalizability of the results, and focusing exclusively on elderly patients with PFFs may limit the applicability of the findings to other age groups or different types of fractures. Collectively, these limitations indicate that the prognostic value of the HALP score requires further validation in large-scale studies that include diverse populations.

ops.markdown: In a study by Balta et al., CRP-based biomarkers (CRP, CAR and the CRP-to-lymphocyte ratio) predicted 30-day mortality after hip fracture surgery in elderly patients, prompting the authors to recommend routine preoperative CRP and albumin assessment [42]. Another study likewise linked high CAR values to an increased mortality risk in hip fracture patients [43]. In our cohort, CRP and CAR were both statistically significant predictors, yet the HALP score had higher predictive power for 30-day and 1-year mortality, and its 1-year survival analysis was statistically more significant than those of the other biomarkers. The HALP score may thus help distinguish survivors from non-survivors at the 1-year mortality point and assist clinicians in planning treatment and allocating resources for elderly patients with PFFs; with further validation across diverse populations and healthcare settings, it could become a standard assessment method in geriatric orthopedic care.
